q: What is the regulatory classification of the FOM?
a: It is classified as an FAA-accepted manual with approved content.

src.quote: The FOM is classified as an FAA-accepted manual with approved content.
src.note: The FOM is an accepted manual, but portions of its content are FAA-approved. Publication follows the FAA Approval/Acceptance Request Process defined in the Company Administrative Manual.

q: Per the FOM, who has the authority and responsibility to deviate from published guidance in the interest of safety, and under which regulations?
a: The PIC, as set forth in CFR 91.3 and 121.557.

src.quote: As set forth in CFR 91.3 and 121.557, the PIC has the authority and responsibility to deviate from published guidance to the extent required in the interest of safety.
src.note: The manual cannot anticipate every situation, so the PIC retains deviation authority scoped to what safety requires.

q: If a conflict exists between Company manuals, what hierarchy applies?
a: F&F/Company NOTAMs, then Required Operational Memos, then 10-7 information.

src.quote: If a conflict exists between Company manuals, the following hierarchy applies:
src.note: The listed order ranks the sources: F&F/Company NOTAMs are highest, followed by Required Operational Memos, then 10-7 information.

q: When manual guidance conflicts, which guidance governs?
a: The more restrictive guidance will apply.

src.quote: In the event of conflicting manual guidance, the more restrictive guidance will apply.
src.note: This 'most restrictive wins' rule also reappears in 1.5 for conflicting directives across the Company Manual System.

q: How are incremental revisions to the FOM numbered?
a: Numbered subsequent to the current revision (123.1, 123.2) until the next full revision.

src.quote: An incremental revision will be numbered subsequent to the current revision (e.g., 123.1, 123.2) until the next full revision (e.g., 124, 125), and will retain the change bars from the current full revision.
src.note: Incremental revisions push out information earlier than a full revision allows, or for content with a specific effective date, and keep the current full revision's change bars.

q: By what means are changes to regulatory information conveyed to crews?
a: By Required Operational Memo, Field & Facility (F&F)/Company NOTAMs, and Manual Revision or Incremental Revision.

src.quote: Alaska Airlines is responsible for timely dissemination of all regulatory information required for safe, compliant flight operations.
src.note: Regulatory changes use those three channels; administrative information instead goes out by Informational Memo and Company email.

q: In the FOM's conventions, what do the words 'Shall' or 'Must' indicate?
a: That a procedure, practice, or condition is mandatory.

src.quote: “Shall” or “Must” indicates that a procedure, practice, or condition is mandatory.
src.note: By contrast 'Should' means recommended, and 'May' or 'Need not' means optional.

q: What does the word 'Should' indicate in this manual, versus 'May' or 'Need not'?
a: 'Should' indicates a procedure, practice, or condition is recommended; 'May' or 'Need not' indicates it is optional.

src.quote: “Should” indicates that a procedure, practice, or condition is recommended.
src.note: Three tiers: mandatory (Shall/Must), recommended (Should), optional (May/Need not).

q: What is the difference between a WARNING and a CAUTION in the FOM?
a: WARNING: may result in injury or death. CAUTION: may result in damage to equipment.

src.quote: An operating procedure, practice, or condition that may result in injury or death if not carefully observed or followed.
src.note: WARNING is about people (injury or death); CAUTION is about equipment damage; a Note simply adds emphasis or explanation.

q: What are the three phases of the 'Ready, SAFE, Go' model?
a: Am I Ready?, Is Everything SAFE?, and Can I Go?

src.quote: This phase focuses on your preparation. Before you act, ensure you are ready and have the right resources.
src.note: Ready = preparation and resources; SAFE = self-assess for hazards and act to prevent adverse outcomes; Go = proceed with a safety focus without rushing.

q: What are the four pillars of Alaska's SMS?
a: Safety Policy, Safety Risk Management, Safety Assurance, and Safety Promotion.

src.quote: A process within our SMS that describes a system, identifies any associated hazards, and analyzes, assesses, and controls risk to as low as reasonably practicable.
src.note: Safety Risk Management controls risk to as low as reasonably practicable; the four pillars together form the SMS framework.

q: Who owns the SMS at AAG?
a: The AAG Accountable Executives: Jason Berry for Alaska Airlines, Andy Schneider for Horizon Air.

src.quote: The AAG Accountable Executives own the SMS and are responsible for ensuring its design and performance.
src.note: Ownership formally rests with the Accountable Executives, but the manual stresses each teammate OWNS SAFETY.

q: Who is responsible for the overall content and quality of the FOM?
a: The Managing Director, Standards, Fleet, and Operational Control.

src.quote: The Managing Director, Standards, Fleet, and Operational Control is responsible for the overall content and quality of this manual.
src.note: Two distinct roles: one owns content and quality, the other holds authority to change policies and procedures.

q: Where can questions about this manual's content or suggested improvements be sent?
a: To flightstandards@alaskaair.com.

src.quote: Questions about the content of this manual or suggested improvements should be sent to flightstandards@alaskaair.com.
src.note: This is the single feedback channel for FOM content questions and improvement suggestions.

q: What is the purpose of airline identifiers such as (AS) and (HA) in the manual?
a: They distinguish differences in policies and procedures between Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines.

src.quote: Airline identifiers are used to distinguish the differences in policies and procedures for Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines.
src.note: Placed after a heading when the whole topic is airline-specific, or before content in a paragraph when only that portion applies; a color-filled end box (AS or HA) may be used.

q: Where are terms and definitions used in this manual found?
a: AIM Pilot/Controller Glossary, Jeppesen General Airway Manual Introduction, and 14 CFR Part 1; unique terms in Chapter 26.

src.quote: Terms and definitions used within this manual can be found in the Pilot/Controller Glossary of the AIM, the Introduction of the Jeppesen General Airway Manual, and 14 CFR Part 1.
src.note: General definitions live in those three external sources; manual-specific terms and acronyms are consolidated in Chapter 26.

q: What constraint always overrides Green Policy fuel-saving guidance?
a: Safety. Fuel saving measures must never compromise safety under any circumstances.

src.quote: Fuel saving measures must never compromise safety under any circumstances.
src.note: Green guidance is marked with a symbol and targets fleet-wide fuel savings, but never at the expense of safety.

q: Under Compliance with Regulations, what happens in the event of conflicting directives?
a: The more restrictive directive will apply.

src.quote: In the event of conflicting directives, the more restrictive directive will apply.
src.note: Operations must comply with all applicable Laws, Regulations, Operations Specifications, and the CMS; no regulation or policy replaces sound judgment and a commitment to safety.

q: Where can teammates file safety reports?
a: Virtual Safety Center, safety reporting apps on company mobile devices, Alaska's World Vendor Portal, and the Safety Hotline.

src.quote: AAG has provided a non-punitive safety reporting system for all teammates and business partners.
src.note: The system is non-punitive so long as the teammate was not engaged in unacceptable behaviors, and offers four filing channels.

q: What behaviors are defined as 'unacceptable' and therefore outside safety-reporting protection?
a: Illegal activities, intentional disregard for safety/regulations/policies/procedures, drug and alcohol use, workplace violence, reckless or willful misconduct, falsification of records.

src.quote: Unacceptable behaviors are defined as illegal activities, intentional disregard for safety, regulations, policies, or procedures, drug and alcohol use, workplace violence, reckless conduct and/or willful misconduct, and falsification of records.
src.note: These are established in the AAG Code of Conduct and Ethics; filing a report otherwise will not result in discipline.

q: No FOM procedure covers your situation and the nearest one would be unsafe. What does the FOM authorize the PIC to do?
a: Deviate from published guidance to the extent required in the interest of safety, per CFR 91.3 and 121.557.

src.quote: As set forth in CFR 91.3 and 121.557, the PIC has the authority and responsibility to deviate from published guidance to the extent required in the interest of safety.
src.note: Deviation authority is not a blank check; it is bounded by 'to the extent required in the interest of safety,' and the FOM's philosophy supports decisions that serve the intent of the highest level of operational safety when published guidance is inadequate or inappropriate.

q: Two Company manuals give conflicting guidance for the same task. Which guidance applies?
a: The more restrictive guidance.

src.quote: In the event of conflicting manual guidance, the more restrictive guidance will apply.
src.note: The 'most restrictive wins' rule appears twice, 1.1.1 for conflicting manual guidance and 1.5 for conflicting directives, so conflict always resolves toward the stricter standard.

q: After a flight you realize a procedural step was missed, with no damage or injury. What does the FOM say to do?
a: File a safety report through the non-punitive safety reporting system.

src.quote: Reporting close calls and procedural non-compliance is also critical.
src.note: Protection is non-punitive as long as you were not engaged in unacceptable behaviors; close calls and non-compliance are early warning signs that let the Company fix problems before something worse happens.
